assignment_title: Engineering Design Process - Research, Brainstorming, and Redesign
student_packet_summary: 10 student evidence sets were identified: 9 Slowest Marble packets and 1 Long Span packet. Feedback emphasizes the teacher-selected Research, Brainstorming, and Make It Better sections.
set1_focus: Use cause-and-effect research, genuinely different brainstorms, and test evidence to justify a specific redesign.

students.name: Dean
strengths: Identified relevant motion factors, including slope, turns, and the risk of the marble stopping.
Generated two visibly different brainstorm directions before selecting a prototype.
Used Version 1 experience to simplify and support the redesign rather than merely rebuilding the same idea.
improvements: Make research notes more explicit by writing each factor as a cause-and-effect claim.
In Make It Better, name the exact test observation first, then connect each change to the problem it is meant to solve.
students.feedback: Your design thinking is visible across research, brainstorming, and redesign. The next step is to make the evidence chain clearer: observation -> specific change -> predicted effect.
students.highest_leverage_need: State the test evidence before explaining the redesign.
students.practice_intro: Practice making the link from an observed failure to a precise design change.

practice_questions.label: Cause and effect
practice_questions.prompt: Rewrite this note as a cause-and-effect research claim: turns. Include what kind of turn you mean and what you predict could happen to the marble.

practice_questions.label: Evidence-based redesign
practice_questions.prompt: A trial stops when the marble gets stuck at a tight spiral. Write one specific redesign and explain how that change addresses the observed failure.

practice_questions.label: Compare alternatives
practice_questions.prompt: Compare a spiral path and a switchback path for a slow-marble challenge. Give one possible advantage and one possible risk for each, then choose one to test first and justify your choice.

students.name: Natalie (surname unclear)
students.evidence_pages: Pages 3-4 - Slowest Marble; handwritten surname unclear
strengths: Named several possible motion factors before building, including hills, bumps, and having enough speed.
Produced two brainstorm sketches and a final prototype plan.
improvements: Expand research notes so each factor includes how it could change travel time or reliability.
Make the two brainstorm ideas more clearly different in structure or motion strategy.
Complete Make It Better with a readable, specific change tied to Version 1 evidence.
students.feedback: There is a useful start to the design process, especially in the early planning. Stronger evidence will come from explaining why each research factor matters and documenting a clear redesign after testing.
students.highest_leverage_need: Complete a specific, evidence-linked Make It Better explanation.
students.practice_intro: Focus on turning short design notes into clear engineering reasoning.

practice_questions.label: Research explanation
practice_questions.prompt: For each factor, explain how it could affect the marble: (a) bumps in the track, (b) slope angle, and (c) side walls.

practice_questions.label: Distinct brainstorms
practice_questions.prompt: Describe two genuinely different ways to make a marble take longer to reach the finish. The two ideas must use different path strategies.

practice_questions.label: Make It Better
practice_questions.prompt: Version 1 repeatedly gets stuck halfway down the track. Write a complete redesign statement using: Because the test showed ___, I will change ___, which should ___.

students.name: Chase D
strengths: Research notes clearly connected smoothness, path shape, and failure conditions to marble motion.
Brainstorm sketches explored two path patterns and included start/end thinking.
The redesign directly addressed test evidence that the marble was sticking on rough tape.
improvements: When a redesign makes the marble faster, explain the tradeoff between reliability and the challenge goal of maximizing time.
Use the test numbers to compare whether the redesign improved the intended performance, not only whether it worked.
students.feedback: You used the engineering cycle well: research informed the design, testing identified a concrete problem, and the redesign targeted that problem. Push the analysis further by evaluating both reliability and travel time after a change.
students.highest_leverage_need: Evaluate redesign tradeoffs using both success and travel-time evidence.
students.practice_intro: Extend your strong evidence use by analyzing tradeoffs and optimization.

practice_questions.label: Tradeoff analysis
practice_questions.prompt: Version 1 takes 9.7 s but sticks in 1 of 3 trials. Version 2 takes 8.8 s and succeeds in all 3 trials. Explain the tradeoff and decide what you would change next.

practice_questions.label: Optimization
practice_questions.prompt: Suggest one change that could increase travel time without reintroducing the rough-surface problem. Explain the mechanism.

practice_questions.label: Evidence claim
practice_questions.prompt: Write a CER-style claim about whether a smoother track was an improvement. Use both reliability and time as evidence.

students.name: Kai
strengths: Research was specific and causal, naming slope, friction, momentum, alignment, and failure risks.
Two substantially different brainstorm concepts were developed before building.
The redesign responded to the marble leaving the intended path by changing the track orientation.
improvements: After redesigning, compare Version 1 and Version 2 data more explicitly to decide whether the change actually improved performance.
Separate reliability improvements from speed/travel-time improvements when evaluating the result.
students.feedback: Your pre-build thinking is detailed and shows strong engineering awareness. The next level is closing the loop after testing: use the Version 2 data to judge whether the predicted effect occurred and what should change next.
students.highest_leverage_need: Use Version 2 evidence to evaluate the redesign, not just describe it.
students.practice_intro: Practice evaluating whether a redesign actually produced its predicted effect.

practice_questions.label: Prediction and result
practice_questions.prompt: A redesign is intended to keep the marble on the track, but the best successful time stays the same. Explain how the redesign could still be partly successful.

practice_questions.label: Data evaluation
practice_questions.prompt: Version 1: 2 of 3 successful, best time 4.9 s. Version 2: 3 of 3 successful, best time 4.8 s. Write a balanced evaluation using both reliability and travel time.

practice_questions.label: Next iteration
practice_questions.prompt: Propose one next redesign that might increase time while keeping the reliability gained in Version 2. Explain why it should work.

students.name: Jackson
students.evidence_pages: Pages 9-10 - Slowest Marble; Days 2-3 page has no written name
strengths: Brainstorm sketches explored more than one path concept.
The redesign recognized that the structure repeatedly fell apart and needed greater strength.
improvements: Research notes should focus on factors that affect motion and reliability, not only restating size requirements.
Make brainstorm ideas easier to compare by labeling the key feature of each design.
Replace broad redesign language such as 'stronger structure' with the exact structural change and why it addresses the failure.
students.feedback: The testing revealed a real failure mode, but the written engineering reasoning is too general to show exactly how the next design will improve. Add cause-and-effect research and make the redesign specific enough that another person could build it.
students.highest_leverage_need: Turn general ideas into specific cause-and-effect design decisions.
students.practice_intro: Focus on distinguishing requirements from research and making redesigns buildable and specific.

practice_questions.label: Requirement or research?
practice_questions.prompt: Classify each statement as a requirement or a research/design factor: (a) base must fit in 12 in x 12 in, (b) a wider base may improve stability, (c) maximum height is 36 in, (d) tighter turns may increase derailment risk.

practice_questions.label: Specific redesign
practice_questions.prompt: A cardboard tower falls apart where two track sections meet. Replace 'make it stronger' with one specific structural change and explain why it should help.

practice_questions.label: Label the idea
practice_questions.prompt: Describe two different track ideas. For each, label the feature that is supposed to slow the marble and one likely failure risk.

students.name: Nelson Bond
students.evidence_pages: Pages 11-12 - Slowest Marble; Days 2-3 page has no written name
strengths: Research included useful design thinking about small slopes and reducing tape-related friction.
Brainstorm sketches considered clearly different structural approaches and included dimensions/features.
The redesign proposed simplifying the structure rather than adding complexity.
improvements: Record Version 1 test evidence before choosing a redesign so the change can be justified from observed behavior.
Explain how the simpler/open design is expected to affect travel time, reliability, or build quality.
students.feedback: Your planning shows solid design thinking, but the missing test record breaks the evidence chain. A strong Make It Better section should begin with what happened in Version 1 and then explain how the chosen change targets that result.
students.highest_leverage_need: Document test evidence before selecting and justifying the redesign.
students.practice_intro: Practice using observed test data as the reason for a redesign.

practice_questions.label: Evidence first
practice_questions.prompt: Write three observations you would record during a marble test so they could later support a redesign decision.

practice_questions.label: Match evidence to change
practice_questions.prompt: Evidence: the marble stops at taped seams but never leaves the track. Choose a specific redesign and explain why it matches the evidence.

practice_questions.label: Redesign statement
practice_questions.prompt: Use the frame Because ___ happened in Version 1, I will ___, which should ___. Write a complete statement for a structure that is too complicated to build accurately.

students.name: Landon (surname unclear)
strengths: Recognized slope angle as an important factor in controlling marble speed.
The Make It Better sketch and note attempted to correct the marble falling off the rails.
improvements: Research at least two or three interacting factors, such as slope, friction, turns, walls, and alignment.
Develop two complete brainstorm ideas before choosing one; the second brainstorm space was not used.
Explain why the redesign change should fix the observed failure rather than only naming the change.
students.feedback: You identified one important factor and one useful failure to address. To show the full engineering process, broaden the research, create a real alternative during brainstorming, and explain the predicted effect of the redesign.
students.highest_leverage_need: Generate and compare two complete alternatives before selecting a design.
students.practice_intro: Build stronger early-stage design thinking before moving to the final solution.

practice_questions.label: Research factors
practice_questions.prompt: List three factors that can affect marble travel time or reliability. For each, write one predicted effect.

practice_questions.label: Two alternatives
practice_questions.prompt: Sketch in words two different solutions for slowing a marble: one based on path length and one based on changing slope/turn geometry.

practice_questions.label: Explain the redesign
practice_questions.prompt: The marble falls off the outside of a turn. Propose one change and explain exactly how it reduces that failure risk.

students.name: Hayden
strengths: Produced two bridge/span brainstorm sketches and selected a prototype direction.
After the first test, proposed adding straws to the bottom as a possible structural improvement.
improvements: Complete the research section with ideas about shape, joints, bending, bracing, and load paths before building.
Use the first test result to identify a specific weakness even when the structure did not fully fail.
Explain why added material at the bottom should improve the span instead of only naming the change.
students.feedback: The visual ideas are a useful start, but the written engineering reasoning is incomplete. Research and test observations should tell you where the structure is weak so the redesign targets a specific load-path or bending problem.
students.highest_leverage_need: Add pre-build research and identify a specific structural weakness from testing.
students.practice_intro: Apply the same research-evidence-redesign chain to a structural engineering problem.

practice_questions.label: Structural research
practice_questions.prompt: Explain how each could affect a long-span structure: (a) diagonal bracing, (b) weak joints, and (c) bending at midspan.

practice_questions.label: Observe before redesign
practice_questions.prompt: A span holds the load but bends noticeably in the middle. Write the most useful test observation and one specific redesign that targets it.

practice_questions.label: Load-path reasoning
practice_questions.prompt: Explain why adding a bottom member or diagonal brace could help a structure carry a hanging load. Use the idea of spreading or redirecting forces.

students.name: Cheyenne Martin
students.evidence_pages: Pages 19-20 - Slowest Marble; Days 2-3 page marked absent
strengths: Research was specific and causal, addressing slope, friction, turns, path length, and failure conditions.
Two distinct brainstorm ideas were clearly sketched and the selected solution was justified by path length and time.
improvements: The Make It Better section was not observed because the Days 2-3 page was marked absent; complete the test-redesign portion when evidence is available.
When returning to the task, use actual test observations to decide whether to adjust slope, friction, path length, or containment.
students.feedback: Your research and brainstorming provide strong evidence of early-stage engineering thinking. The current evidence cannot show the redesign step, so the next priority is to complete testing and an evidence-based Make It Better decision.
students.highest_leverage_need: Complete the test-and-redesign cycle using actual trial evidence.
students.practice_intro: Your early design reasoning is strong; practice closing the engineering loop after testing.

practice_questions.label: Predict test evidence
practice_questions.prompt: For your long-path concept, list three observations you would collect during testing that would help you decide what to redesign.

practice_questions.label: Choose from evidence
practice_questions.prompt: Suppose the marble moves slowly but falls off at the final turn in 2 of 3 trials. Write one redesign that preserves slow travel while improving reliability.

practice_questions.label: Complete the loop
practice_questions.prompt: Write a full Make It Better response using: evidence from Version 1, the specific change, and the predicted result.

students.name: Adam Olson
strengths: Research identified multiple practical factors, including ramps, smooth tracks, walls, and supports.
Brainstormed two different path concepts before selecting a prototype.
Used the failed first trial to add walls, then collected Version 2 evidence showing the change improved reliability and increased the best time from 12 s to 15 s.
improvements: Make the research notes more explicitly causal by stating how each feature is expected to affect speed or failure risk.
Use the improvement calculation and repeated trials to make a stronger final engineering claim.
students.feedback: You completed the strongest evidence loop in the packet: a clear failure was observed, the redesign targeted that failure, and Version 2 data showed improvement. Extend this by quantifying the improvement and explaining the mechanism behind the change.
students.highest_leverage_need: Quantify and explain why the redesign improved the result.
students.practice_intro: Extend strong design-cycle evidence into quantitative engineering analysis.

practice_questions.label: Quantify improvement
practice_questions.prompt: Version 1 best time was 12 s and Version 2 best time was 15 s. Find the increase in seconds and the percent increase relative to Version 1.

practice_questions.label: Mechanism
practice_questions.prompt: Explain why adding side walls can improve reliability without necessarily making the marble move more slowly.

practice_questions.label: Next optimization
practice_questions.prompt: Propose one next change that might increase travel time while keeping the wall-based reliability improvement. State what evidence you would collect to test it.

class_summary.evidence_line: 10 student evidence sets across two engineering mini-challenges
class_summary.evidence_analyzed: The submitted record sheets were reviewed with emphasis on Research / What Should We Think About?, Brainstorming, and Make It Better. No rubric was supplied, so scores are teacher-review recommendations based on completeness, specificity, causal reasoning, and evidence use in those sections.
strengths: Most students generated at least two visual solution ideas before or during prototyping.
Several students identified relevant physical/design variables such as slope, friction, turns, walls, supports, and path length.
The strongest packets used a concrete test failure to drive a targeted redesign rather than simply rebuilding the same design.
needs: Research notes often list nouns or constraints instead of cause-and-effect predictions about performance.
Some brainstorms are variations of the same idea or leave the second alternative incomplete, limiting meaningful comparison.
Make It Better is the clearest class-wide leverage point: students need to cite the exact test observation, name the specific change, and predict its effect.
Several packets record redesign ideas without enough Version 1 evidence to show why that change was selected.
class_summary.highest_leverage_target: Use the evidence chain: 'Because the test showed ___, I will change ___, which should ___.'

groupings.title: Evidence-to-Redesign Support
groupings.students: Natalie, Jackson, Nelson Bond, Landon, Hayden, Cheyenne Martin
groupings.note: Practice recording a specific observation and using it as the reason for a precise Make It Better change.

groupings.title: Research Cause-and-Effect
groupings.note: Turn short notes and constraints into predictions about how variables affect speed, reliability, bending, or failure.

groupings.title: Optimization / Extension
groupings.students: Dean, Chase D, Kai, Adam Olson
groupings.note: Evaluate tradeoffs, quantify improvement, and decide whether a redesign improved the intended success measure as well as reliability.

class_summary.limitations: No scoring rubric was included. Recommendations therefore reflect the teacher-selected evidence sections rather than every field on the packet. One packet is from the Long Span challenge; the same engineering-process criteria were applied. Natalie and Landon have partly unreadable surnames/initials. Cheyenne Martin's Days 2-3 sheet is marked absent, so missing redesign evidence was treated as not observed rather than incorrect.

set1.label: Research: cause and effect
set1.prompt: A marble reaches the finish in 3.2 s but repeatedly leaves the track at a sharp turn. Name one factor that could affect travel time and one factor that could affect reliability. For each factor, state the effect you would predict before rebuilding.
set1.answer: Example: Travel time - slope angle; a steeper slope can increase speed and reduce travel time. Reliability - turn radius or side-wall height; a gentler turn or taller outside wall can reduce derailment. Other well-reasoned factors are valid.
set1.teacher_move: Press students to add the predicted effect after each factor; nouns alone are not enough.
set1.discourse_move: Partners compare factor + predicted effect and ask, 'What makes you think that will happen?'

verification.method: Checked that the sample factors separately address speed/time and staying on the path, with plausible cause-and-effect relationships.

set1.label: Requirement vs. research
set1.prompt:
Which note is a research/design factor rather than a requirement?
A. The base must fit inside 12 in x 12 in.
B. A very shallow slope may slow the marble, but if it is too shallow the marble may stop.
C. The structure must be free-standing.
set1.answer: B. It predicts how a design variable (slope) may affect performance. A and C are requirements/constraints.
set1.teacher_move: Ask students what makes a statement testable or predictive rather than simply a rule to follow.
set1.discourse_move: Students defend the classification by naming the variable and the predicted outcome.

verification.method: Classified A and C as explicit constraints and B as a causal design hypothesis.

set1.label: Brainstorm for difference
set1.prompt: Idea A is a tall zig-zag switchback track. Describe an Idea B that is meaningfully different but still tries to maximize marble travel time. Then name one tradeoff between the two ideas.
set1.answer: Example Idea B: a wide spiral/funnel path. Tradeoff: a spiral can create a long continuous path in less height, but it may be harder to build accurately and may increase derailment or sticking risk. Other genuinely different ideas/tradeoffs are valid.
set1.teacher_move: Reject cosmetic changes as a second idea; look for a different path strategy, geometry, or mechanism.
set1.discourse_move: Students explain what is structurally different between the two ideas before discussing which they prefer.

verification.method: Verified that the example changes the core path strategy and identifies a realistic design tradeoff.

set1.label: Compare brainstorms
set1.prompt:
Two teams propose:
Design A: a long, shallow switchback with side walls.
Design B: a shorter, steeper spiral with no side walls.
If the goal is the longest reliable travel time, choose which one you would prototype first and justify your choice with two engineering factors.
set1.answer: A defensible answer may choose either design if it considers both time and reliability. Example: Design A because the longer/shallow path may increase travel time and side walls may improve reliability. A student could choose B only with a plausible argument and stated risks.
set1.teacher_move: Do not grade the letter choice; grade the quality of the two-factor justification.
set1.discourse_move: Partners challenge one factor in the other's justification and ask for a predicted failure mode.

verification.method: Checked the item as open-response with a criterion-based answer: valid choice requires two relevant factors and explicit reasoning.

set1.label: Evidence to redesign
set1.prompt: Version 1 data: Trial 1 = 8 s, failed at the same sharp turn; Trial 2 = 7 s, failed at that turn; Trial 3 = 6 s, successful. Propose one specific Make It Better change and explain why the test evidence supports it.
set1.answer: Example: increase the turn radius or add/tall-en the outside wall at that turn. The repeated failures occurred at the same location, so changing containment or turn geometry directly targets the observed failure while preserving the rest of the path.
set1.teacher_move: Require students to name the repeated observation before accepting the redesign.
set1.discourse_move: Students use the frame, 'Because the test showed ___, I would change ___, which should ___.'

verification.method: Matched the redesign to the repeated turn failure rather than unrelated parts of the structure.

set1.label: Strong redesign explanation
set1.prompt:
Which Make It Better statement gives stronger engineering evidence, and why?
1. 'I will make the track better.'
2. 'Because the marble left the outside of the second turn in two trials, I will add a taller outside wall there so the marble stays on the path.'
set1.answer: Statement 2. It includes a specific observation, a specific design change, and the predicted effect. Statement 1 is too general to show evidence-based reasoning.
set1.teacher_move: Highlight the three-part chain: observation -> change -> predicted effect.
set1.discourse_move: Students underline the evidence, box the change, and circle the predicted effect in statement 2.

verification.method: Confirmed statement 2 contains all three required parts and statement 1 contains none of them specifically.

set1.label: Transfer: structural redesign
set1.prompt:
A long-span structure holds the load, but the center bends noticeably while the joints remain secure. Which redesign is most directly supported by the evidence?
A. Add diagonal bracing near the center.
B. Add more tape to every joint.
C. Shorten the required span.
Choose and justify.
set1.answer: A. The observed problem is bending at the center, while the joints are already secure. Diagonal bracing targets the weak/deforming region without changing the goal. B does not match the evidence; C changes the challenge rather than improving the design.
set1.teacher_move: Ask, 'What part of the evidence rules out each other option?'
set1.discourse_move: Students eliminate one distractor by citing the evidence before defending the best redesign.

verification.method: Matched center bending to bracing; ruled out joint tape because joints are secure and span reduction because it changes the goal.

set1.label: Evaluate improvement quantitatively
set1.prompt: Version 1 best successful marble time is 12 s. After adding side walls, Version 2 has three successful trials and a best time of 15 s. By how many seconds did the best time improve? What is the percent increase from Version 1? Does the evidence support the redesign? Explain.
set1.answer: Increase = 15 - 12 = 3 s. Percent increase = 3/12 = 0.25 = 25%. Yes: the best time increased by 25% and Version 2 also had three successful trials, so the evidence supports the redesign for both performance and reliability.
set1.teacher_move: Press students to distinguish absolute improvement (3 s) from relative improvement (25%).
set1.discourse_move: Students compare calculations, then connect the number back to the engineering claim in one sentence.

verification.method: Independently computed 15-12=3 and 3/12=0.25=25%; checked the reliability statement against three successful Version 2 trials.

questions.prompt: A marble moves too fast on the first drop. Name one design factor you would research and predict how changing it could affect speed.
questions.answer: Example: reduce the slope angle; a shallower slope can reduce acceleration/speed. Other plausible causal factors are valid.

questions.prompt: Classify: 'The base must fit in 12 in x 12 in.' Is this a requirement or a research factor?
questions.answer: Requirement/constraint.

questions.prompt: Classify: 'Tighter turns may make the marble leave the track.' Is this a requirement or a research factor?
questions.answer: Research/design factor because it predicts how a variable affects performance.

questions.prompt: For a long-span structure, explain one reason diagonal bracing might matter before you build.
questions.answer: It can reduce deformation/racking and help redirect/spread forces through the structure.

questions.prompt: Idea A is a zig-zag ramp. Give a genuinely different Idea B for slowing a marble.
questions.answer: Example: spiral/funnel path, bowl-and-ramp path, or another substantially different geometry.

questions.prompt: Why is changing only the color, tape placement, or small decoration not enough to count as a second engineering brainstorm?
questions.answer: Those changes do not create a meaningfully different solution strategy or performance mechanism.

questions.prompt: Give one advantage and one risk of a long shallow path.
questions.answer: Advantage: may increase travel time. Risk: may stop if too shallow or may require more space/material.

questions.prompt: Give one advantage and one risk of a steep compact path.
questions.answer: Advantage: easier to keep moving / compact. Risk: may be too fast or harder to keep on the path.

questions.prompt: The marble leaves the outside of the same turn in 2 of 3 trials. Propose one specific redesign.
questions.answer: Example: add/tall-en the outside wall or increase the turn radius at that turn.

questions.prompt: The marble sticks at taped seams in repeated trials. Propose one specific redesign.
questions.answer: Smooth/reduce the seams, change how sections join, or move tape away from the rolling surface.

questions.prompt: A bridge holds but bends at midspan while joints stay firm. What should the redesign target?
questions.answer: The midspan/load path, such as adding bracing or strengthening the central members, not the already-secure joints.

questions.prompt: Why is 'make it stronger' weaker than 'add a diagonal brace across the bending side panel'?
questions.answer: The second is specific, buildable, and targets an observed failure mechanism.

questions.prompt: Complete: Because the test showed the marble fell off the final turn twice, I will ___, which should ___.
questions.answer: Example: add a taller outside wall; keep the marble on the path through the turn.

questions.prompt: Complete: Because the structure bent in the center, I will ___, which should ___.
questions.answer: Example: add diagonal/central bracing; reduce bending and spread the load.

questions.prompt: What three parts should a strong Make It Better explanation contain?
questions.answer: Specific test observation/evidence, specific design change, and predicted effect/reason.

questions.prompt: Rewrite 'It did not work, so I changed it' as a stronger evidence-based statement.
questions.answer: Any response that names what failed, the exact change, and why that change should address the failure.

questions.prompt: A marble track and a long-span bridge are different challenges. What part of the engineering process should stay the same after the first test?
questions.answer: Use observed evidence to identify a specific weakness, make a targeted redesign, and retest the predicted effect.

questions.prompt: A marble track is reliable but too fast. A bridge is strong but bends too much. For each, write the performance variable you would target next.
questions.answer: Marble: travel time/speed while preserving reliability. Bridge: stiffness/deformation or load path while preserving span/strength.

questions.prompt: Why can a successful first test still justify a redesign?
questions.answer: A design can meet the minimum requirement but still be optimized for the success measure, efficiency, reliability, or margin.

questions.prompt: Give one example of a redesign that improves one criterion but could hurt another. Name the tradeoff.
questions.answer: Example: making a marble slope steeper improves reliable motion but can reduce travel time; adding material can strengthen a bridge but increase mass/material use.

questions.prompt: Version 1 best time = 10 s; Version 2 best time = 13 s. Find the improvement in seconds.
For the same data (10 s to 13 s), find the percent increase relative to Version 1.
Version 1 succeeds 3/3 trials at 10 s. Version 2 succeeds 1/3 trials at 14 s. Is Version 2 clearly better? Explain.
questions.answer: No. It has a longer successful time but much worse reliability; the evidence shows a tradeoff, not a clear overall improvement.

questions.prompt: A redesign improves reliability but reduces travel time slightly. What additional test or change would you plan next?
questions.answer: Retest multiple trials while adjusting slope/path length/friction to recover time without losing the reliability gain; a specific evidence-based plan is valid.
